In octahedral ruthenium complexes like this one, the three PPh3 ligands can be arranged in different ways:
- All three could be equivalent (all in the same environment)
- Two could be equivalent and one different (two environments)
- All three could be different (three environments)

The most common arrangement for this specific complex [RuH2(CO)(PPh3)3] is that two of the phosphines are in equivalent positions (trans to each other), and the third is in a different position.

In this case:
- The two equivalent phosphorus atoms would couple with the third phosphorus atom
- The single phosphorus atom would couple with the two equivalent phosphorus atoms

When a phosphorus atom couples with n equivalent phosphorus atoms, it splits into (n+1) peaks according to the n+1 rule. So:
- The signal from the two equivalent phosphorus atoms would be split into a doublet (coupling to 1 P atom)
- The signal from the single phosphorus atom would be split into a triplet (coupling to 2 P atoms)

Therefore, we would expect to see a triplet and a doublet in the ^31P NMR spectrum.
